title: Background of Vector Calculus in Mechanics
short_intro: Vector calculus provides the foundational mathematical framework for describing spatial rates of change and integration of physical quantities in mechanics. It enables rigorous formulation of position, velocity, acceleration, and the interaction of forces within scalar and vector fields.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic vector algebra, dot and cross products, scalar and vector point functions, and time derivatives of vectors in cartesian coordinates.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Gradient, divergence, curl, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Gauss's divergence, and Stokes' theorems applied to central forces and gravitational fields.

prerequisites: Differential and integral calculus of single and multiple variables

concept_notes.heading: Scalars and Vectors in Mechanics
bullets: A scalar quantity is completely specified by a magnitude with appropriate units (e.g., mass, energy, time).
A vector quantity possesses both magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle law of addition (e.g., displacement, velocity, force).
In a three-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system, a vector A is expressed as A = A<sub>x</sub> î + A<sub>y</sub> ĵ + A<sub>z</sub> k̂.

concept_notes.heading: Time Derivatives of Vectors
bullets: The time derivative of a vector whose magnitude and direction change with time requires accounting for the rotation of the unit vectors.
For a rotating reference frame, the time derivative of vector A is given by d/dt (A) = (dA/dt)<sub>rel</sub> + ω × A.
This formulation is essential for analyzing kinematics in non-inertial systems, including the derivation of Coriolis and centrifugal forces.

concept_notes.heading: Gradient, Divergence, and Curl
bullets: The gradient of a scalar field φ yields a vector pointing in the direction of the maximum spatial rate of change.
The divergence of a vector field F measures the net outward flux per unit volume from an infinitesimal element, representing sources or sinks.
The curl of a vector field F measures the local rotation or circulation of the field about a point.

concept_notes.heading: Integral Theorems in Mechanics
bullets: Gauss's Divergence Theorem relates the volume integral of the divergence of a vector field to the surface enclosing it.
Stokes' Theorem connects the surface integral of the curl of a vector field over an open surface to the line integral around its boundary curve.
These theorems are directly applied to derive differential forms of conservation laws, such as Gauss's law for gravity.

derivations.title: Time Derivative of a Rotating Unit Vector
derivations.conditions: A unit vector rotating with an angular velocity vector ω about a fixed axis.
steps: Consider a unit vector û rotating in a plane with angular speed dθ/dt = ω.
Express the components of û in Cartesian coordinates as û = cos(θ) î + sin(θ) ĵ.
Differentiate with respect to time t: dû/dt = -sin(θ)(dθ/dt) î + cos(θ)(dθ/dt) ĵ.
Substitute ω and recognize that the resulting vector is perpendicular to û, matching the cross product ω × û.

derivations.title: Conservative Force and Potential Gradient
derivations.conditions: A force field F(r) satisfying ∇ × F = 0.
steps: Define the work done W in moving a particle in a conservative force field as W = ∫ F · dr = - ΔU, where U is potential energy.
Express the infinitesimal change in potential energy as dU = -F · dr = - (F<sub>x</sub> dx + F<sub>y</sub> dy + F<sub>z</sub> dz).
By definition of the total differential of U(x, y, z), dU = (∂U/∂x)dx + (∂U/∂y)dy + (∂U/∂z)dz.
Compare coefficients of dx, dy, and dz to obtain F<sub>x</sub> = -∂U/∂x, etc., leading to vector form.

formula_sheet.name: Gradient of a Scalar Field
formula_sheet.variables: φ = scalar potential function, x, y, z = Cartesian coordinates

formula_sheet.name: Divergence of a Vector Field
formula_sheet.equation_html: \vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{F} = \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial z}
formula_sheet.variables: F = vector field, F<sub>x</sub>, F<sub>y</sub>, F<sub>z</sub> = Cartesian components
formula_sheet.conditions: Vector field must be continuously differentiable

formula_sheet.name: Curl of a Vector Field
formula_sheet.equation_html: \vec{\nabla} \times \vec{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ F_x & F_y & F_z \end{vmatrix}
formula_sheet.conditions: Vector field must be continuously differentiable

formula_sheet.name: Gauss's Divergence Theorem
formula_sheet.variables: V = volume, S = closed surface bounding V, dS outward normal surface element
formula_sheet.units: Integral units depend on field F
formula_sheet.conditions: F and its derivatives must be continuous in V

formula_sheet.name: Stokes' Theorem
formula_sheet.variables: S = open surface, C = boundary curve of S
formula_sheet.units: Integral units depend on field F
formula_sheet.conditions: Surface S and boundary C satisfy Stokes' orientation rules

formula_sheet.name: Coriolis Acceleration
formula_sheet.variables: ω = angular velocity of frame, v<sub>rel</sub> = relative velocity

formula_sheet.name: Central Force Condition
formula_sheet.variables: F = central force vector, r = position vector magnitude
formula_sheet.conditions: Force directed toward or away from a fixed center

graphs_and_experiments.title: Scalar Field Contour Lines and Gradient
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Concentric closed loops representing equipotential contours with orthogonal arrows pointing uphill representing the gradient vector field.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The gradient vector is everywhere perpendicular to the equipotential contour lines and points in the direction of the steepest ascent.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual questions linking potential energy contours to conservative force directions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Physical Interpretation of Divergence
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A small control volume with vector field lines expanding outward (positive divergence) versus contracting inward (negative divergence).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Positive divergence denotes a source where net flux originates; negative divergence denotes a sink where flux terminates.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in questions related to fluid flow continuity and inverse-square central gravitational fields.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Physical Interpretation of Curl
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A vector field showing shear or circular flow around an axis, with a small paddle wheel placed in the flow to indicate rotation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Non-zero curl indicates rotational flow or the presence of a localized vortex; zero curl denotes an irrotational field.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested to distinguish between conservative (irrotational) and non-conservative force fields.

solved_numericals.question: Find the angle between the two vectors A = 2î + 2ĵ - k̂ and B = 6î - 3ĵ + 2k̂.
solution_steps: Calculate the dot product: A · B = (2)(6) + (2)(-3) + (-1)(2) = 12 - 6 - 2 = 4.
Use the dot product formula cos(θ) = (A · B) / (|A||B|) = 4 / (3 × 7) = 4/21.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the divergence and curl of the vector field F = xz<sup>3</sup> î - 2x<sup>2</sup>yz ĵ + 2pz<sup>2</sup>k̂ at point (1, -1, 1).
solution_steps: Identify components: F<sub>x</sub> = xz<sup>3</sup>, F<sub>y</sub> = -2x<sup>2</sup>yz, F<sub>z</sub> = 2yz<sup>2</sup> (taking standard scalar parameters).

solved_numericals.question: Show that the force field F = yz î + xz ĵ + xy k̂ is conservative and find its corresponding scalar potential U.
solution_steps: Compute curl of F: ∇ × F = î(∂/∂y(xy) - ∂/∂z(xz)) - ĵ(∂/∂x(xy) - ∂/∂z(yz)) + k̂(∂/∂x(xz) - ∂/∂y(yz)) = î(x - x) - ĵ(y - y) + k̂(z - z) = 0.
Since ∇ × F = 0, the force field is conservative.
Differentiate U with respect to y and equate to -F<sub>y</sub>: -∂U/∂y = xz + ∂f/∂y = xz ⇒ ∂f/∂y = 0.
Integrate with respect to z to confirm consistency, yielding U = -xyz + C.

assumptions_and_limitations: Vector calculus operations assume space is continuous and differentiable.
Cartesian coordinate formulations presume an inertial reference frame unless fictitious forces are explicitly introduced via rotating frame transformations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The cross product of two vectors is another vector with commutative properties (A × B = B × A).
common_misconceptions.correct: The cross product is anti-commutative: A × B = -(B × A).
common_misconceptions.why: Reversing the vector order reverses the direction of the resultant vector according to the right-hand rule.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Any arbitrary force field can be expressed as the negative gradient of a scalar potential.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only conservative (irrotational) force fields can be expressed as F = -∇U.
common_misconceptions.why: Non-conservative forces like friction have non-zero curl (∇ × F ≠ 0) and cannot be derived from a single scalar potential.

quick_revision: Gradient converts a scalar to a vector; divergence and curl operate on vector fields via dot and cross products with the del operator.
Gradient of a Scalar Field: \vec{\nabla}\phi = \hat{i}\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} + \hat{j}\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y} + \hat{k}\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z}
Divergence of a Vector Field: \vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{F} = \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial z}
